rows.title: Introduction to Asian American Studies
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome

Critically analyze the intersection of race and racism as they relate to class, gender, sexuality, religion, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, sovereignty, language, and/or age in cultural productions produced by Asian/Asian American artists.

Analyze and articulate concepts such as race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self- determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism as analyzed in relation to the theoretical foundations of the history and development of Asian/Asian American Studies.

Apply theory and knowledge produced by Asian/Asian American communities to describe the critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, lived-experiences, and social struggles of those groups with a particular emphasis on agency and group-affirmation.

Critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Asian/Asian American are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, and language policies.
Describe and actively engage with anti-racist and anti-colonial issues and the practices and movements in Asian/Asian American communities to build a just and equitable society.
Examine the political dimensions during the The Asian American Movement (activism) included but not limited to anti-racism, anti-colonial, student activism, and political art.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Identify major debates, key concepts, influential scholars/thinkers, and current issues in the field of Asian/Asian American Studies.
Survey the immigration, settlement, acculturation, and assimilation of Asian Americans in the U.S.
Examine the contributions of Asian/Asian Americans in American society and their changing roles in socio-political and economic arenas.
Analyze and discuss the Asian Americans and contemporary issues.
Evaluate issues taking an intersectional approach considering race, class, sexuality, and gender.

Analyze Asian American histories and contemporary issues within a global context i.e. consider local dynamics as part of the relationship between Asia and the United States as well as with the Americas.
Analyze race relations between Asian, Blacks, Mexicans and Whites in the U.S.
Define and deconstruct the "model minority myth."
Evaluate the Asian American Movement and activists that impacted Asian American civil rights in the U.S.
Examine and distinguish between the various racial terms used with the Pan-ethnic category "Asian."
Gender analyis on women in the Asian/Asian American community.
Identify and analyze the history and contemporary impact of colonialism, imperialism, and racism on the Asian/Asian American community.
Identify and anaylze the impacts of white racism (anti-Asian sentiment) on the Asian/Asian American community in the U.S.
Examine various artistic styles and eras of Asian/Asian American artists and their cultural signifigance.
Analyze the politicized art and poetic works from the Asian American Movement of the 1960-70s.
Define sexuality and examine issues as they pertain to Asian/Asian American communities.

rows.title: American Culture and Identity
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Critically examine the theories and factors that influence various interpretations of American cultural identity.
Analyze changes in American society and culture, as reflected in artistic styles and forms.
Critically examine the impact of American culture in contemporary global conversations.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Identify theories from various academic disciplines - such as the social sciences, behavioral sciences, or humanities - and apply them to an analysis of American culture and identity.
Students will be able articulate a complex understanding of the factors that influence American cultural identity: including race, gender, sexuality, ability, economic status and citizenship.
Students will analyze histories and narratives of the American past to gain a critical understanding of current issues.
Students will critically engage literature and the arts to analyze the ways in which they reflect changing beliefs, social institutions and identity in America.
Students will investigate and engage in conversations regarding the impact of American values and cultural practices on global communities.

Through a close reading of diverse texts including personal and cultural materials, students will learn how to critically analyze how individuals, groups, and a wide variety of political, economic, and cultural institutions have interacted to shape and give meaning to American Culture and Identity.

rows.title: Introduction to African American Studies
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome

Students will analyze and articulate foundational concepts within the Ethnic Studies discipline, including: race and racism, racialization, ethnicity, equity, ethno-centrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization, sovereignty, imperialism, settler colonialism, and anti-racism as analyzed in Africana Studies.

Students will apply theory and knowledge produced by African American communities to describe the critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, lived-experiences and social struggles of those groups with a particular emphasis on agency and group-affirmation.

Students will critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by African Americans, are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in migration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, language policies.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:

Explain the origins and relevance of African American Studies as an academic discipline and analyze the ways in which its interdisciplinary scope has affected the development of topics and trends in the field;

Present a timeline to illustrate the experience of African Americans from the colonial period through the Civil War and Reconstruction, Feminist movements, World Wars, the Civil Rights movement, Black Power movement, the LGTBQ movement, and the struggles and accomplishments of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries;
Use historical and current data to assess contemporary issues related to African Americans in politics, economics, business, culture, and academia;
Analyze the history of African American artistic, musical, and literary expressions from its African origins to the present;
Evaluate contemporary academic, political, and intellectual challenges and possibilities facing African American Studies;
Discuss the historical and political conditions underlying African American relations with other ethnic American groups.

rows.title: Machine Woodworking/Furniture
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Identify different types of carcass construction and determine the proper use of solid wood versus sheet goods.
Develop, draw and construct a specific piece of carcass furniture which includes a drawer and a door.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Design and construct a basic cabinet, compatible with current industrial standards.
Apply construction methods relevant to current industrial standards.
Compare and contrast joinery as used in the cabinet industry.
Utilize skills necessary to safely operate basic tools, machinery and other equipment necessary to solve basic joinery, milling and construction problems.
Identify and analyze wood and man-made materials as they are related to design and function problems inherent in construction of furniture.

rows.title: Programming Fundamentals I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Develop algorithms for solving simple programming problems.
Describe the mechanics of parameter passing.
Demonstrate in a computer program the properties of a variable such as its associated address, value, scope, persistence, and size.
Design, implement, test, and debug a program written in a high level programming language.
Demonstrate the following fundamental programming constructs: basic computation, simple I/O, standard conditional and iterative structures, and functions.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Describe the software development life-cycle;
Explain what an algorithm is and its importance in computer programming;
Describe the principles of structured programming;

Design, implement, test and debug a program that uses each of the following fundamental programming constructs: basic computation, simple I/O, sequence, selection and iteration, functions, arrays, strings, and structures;
Utilize pseudocode or a programming language to implement, test, and debug algorithms for solving simple problems;
Demonstrate different forms of binding, visibility, scoping, and lifetime management.

rows.title: Basic Economics
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
The student will draw demand and supply curves, label them correctly and use the graphs to explain fluctuating prices of a commodity - for example gasoline.
The students will be able to explain the role of competition in the American economy.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:

Illustrate understanding of the relevance of economics in their daily life by analyzing current events. They will clearly delineate the difference between fact and opinion and identify the assumptions upon which conclusions are based.
Identify the types of markets and illustrate how differences in the markets affect their production and consumption patterns.
Use economic theory to explore macroeconomic issues.
Evaluate the cost and benefits of global trade

rows.title: Fire Protection Organization
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Illustrate the history of the fire service.
Compare and contrast effective management concepts for various emergency situations.
Analyze careers in fire and emergency services.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Illustrate and explain the history.
Evaluate the culture of the fire service.
Analyze the basic components of fire as a chemical chain reaction, as well as the major phases of fire.
Examine the main factors that influence fire spread and fire behavior.
List and describe the major organizations tha provide emergency response service, and illustrate how they interrelate.
Explain the scope, purpose, and organizational structure of fire and emergency services.
Differentiate between fire service training and education.
Explain the value of higher education to the professionalization of the fire service.
Define the role of national, state, and local support organizations in fire and emergency services.
Describe the common types of fire and emergency services facilities, equipment and apparatus.
Compare and contrast effective management concepts for various emergency situations.
Identify fire protection and emergency service careers in both the public and private sector.
Expain the primary responsibility of fire prevention personnel, including code enforcement, public information, and publice and private protection systems.
Develop the components of career preparation and goal setting.
Demonstrate the importance of wellness and fitness as it relates to emergency services.

rows.title: Health Education and Fitness Dynamics
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Apply the dimensions of wellness to their lives and explain how integrating these dimensions can increase their overall, lifelong wellness.
Identify and define preventative strategies for chronic diseases including heart disease, stroke, cancer and diabetes.
Describe how healthy behaviors contribute to promoting social wellness and public health.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Describe the 6 dimensions of wellness (physical, emotional, intellectual, social, spiritual and environmental) and their interrelationship.
Distinguish the difference between personal health and public health.

Identify concepts of the physical qualities of health, i.e: fitness, skill performance, body mechanics, posture, obesity, stress, diet, nutrition, exercise values as they relate to students' physical well-being towards lifelong wellness.
Identify programs for aiding students in becoming physically fit and more efficient in their daily life.
Describe the role of stress and mental health in health promotion and disease prevention.
Identify fitness principles and exercise program components to improve cardiorespiratiory endurance, muscular strength and endurance, flexiblity and body composition.

Evaluate the student’s attitude toward health, physical activity, physical dependency, substance abuse, stress induced behavior, building self esteem and relationships to develop a better understanding of one's social, intellectual and emotional well being.
Apply the dietary recommendations to diet planning in the promotion of weight management, physical fitness and disease prevention.
Examine individual and family health behaviors in relation to human sexuality, relationships, sexual orientation, and parenting.

Identify preventative measures for various diseases, infections, cancer, communicable, and cardiovascular diseases in order to acquire a better appreciation of the social, emotional and intellectual implications they have on one’s quality of health.
Describe the role of substance use, misuse, and abuse in our society and its impact on the individual, family, community, economy, and social structure.
Examine factors that lead to violence, substance abuse, addiction and preventative strategies
Identify sexual health practices and methods of contraception related to preventing sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancies.
Describe stimuli leading to types of violence and strategies to minimize its occurrence and promote personal safety.
Identify common practices and attitudes that contribute to intentional and unintentional injuries on a personal and community level and strategies that would reduce their occurrences.
Examine the physiological, emotional, psychological, and sexual aspects of aging.
Examine the connection between eating disorders and body image, and the influence of the media.
Describe the connection and correlation between human beings and their environment.
Analyze the health care system, including inequities and discrepancies.
Interpret and evaluate health and medical information from general and subject-specific library and credible Internet sources.

rows.title: Newswriting and Reporting
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Use and evaluate technologies that enhance the news writing process.
Write a basic, hard-news lead based on proper journalism style.
Explain the role of ethics in their daily work and describe the ethical dimensions of the media's role in society.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Identify and define the principles of journalism.
Demonstrate proficiency in basic journalistic skills through interpretive and accurate news writing and reporting.
In written news accounts, demonstrate the ability to evaluate and organize information.
Distinguish factual statements from judgmental statements and knowledge from opinion.
Effectively evaluate news sources and identify productive newsgathering techniques.
Discover and evaluate outside sources for use in writing editorials for the print media.
Analyze and apply principles of press law and ethics.
Compare and contrast current journalistic theories, methods and techniques.
Use and evaluate technologies that enhance the news writing process.
Learn to write a basic, hard-news lead based on proper journalism Associated Press style.
Conduct research through public documents, web, sources, etc.
Learn effective interviewing techniques.
Learn to write news and feature leads in journalism style.
Learn to write in different journalism forms, including inverted pyramid, martini glass and kabob styles.
Write on deadline.
Write for multiple platforms, web, print, broadcast, PR, etc.

rows.title: Music Appreciation
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Students can articulate two basic elements of style of each of the Baroque, Classic, Romantic, and 20th Century eras.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Compare and contrast the literature of music, its styles, forms, vocabulary and other aspects that contribute to a basic knowledge of music;
Critically analyze the cultural and historic roles played by musicians in history and today, and the role that various technological changes have played in those roles;
Analyze musical pieces of different periods of Western history through listening;
Compare and contrast musical instruments, their sounds, and place in standard ensembles;
Identify through broad historical survey presented in class five or six composers representing the main style periods in Western music;
Apply analytical listening skills while attending a live music concert.

rows.title: Introduction to Political Science
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Define various theories and concepts of politics, political behavior among actors, ideology and political systems.

Interpret the fundamental differences between revolutionary movements that lead to autocratic change and those reform movements that lead toward democratization. A student will analyze the various types of liberal democratic political system.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Identify the main sub fields of political science and describe the various methodologies used in the field.
Analyze the process of political socialization and identify the ways in which children and adults acquire and maintain political orientations;
Examine the concepts of personal and political power;
Analyze mainstream as well as extremist political ideologies in order to evaluate these beliefs and their power in the political world;
Evaluate the ways in which the electronic media shapes our views and understandings about politics;
Identify the paradoxes of nationalism as a political ideology;
Compare and contrast presidential and parliamentary democratic systems;
Compare and contrast authoritarian and totalitarian political systems;
Identify the characteristics of Nazism and the events leading to the holocaust;
Analyze political issues facing third and fourth world countries;
Explore the issue of violence within the USA;
Analyze the causes of international terrorism;
Identify theories about the cause of war;
Analyze the domestic consequences of the cold war and the arms race;
Explain methods of conflict resolution and strategies used to enhance cooperation;

rows.title: Spanish I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Outcome
Demonstrate comprehension of elementary-level spoken Spanish relating to daily activities described in the present tense.
Produce a brief narrative in the present tense describing people and activities, demonstrating a command of basic vocabulary and structures in the Spanish language.
Specific Course Objectives
Objective
Upon successful completion of the course, the student will be able to:
Interact in oral exchange at the elementary level and with appropriate pronunciation and intonation. Exchange greetings and salutations, respond to classroom directions, and ask and answer questions.
Communicate orally and in writing to describe a variety of real-life activities using idiomatic expressions and elementary-level structures in the present tense.
Describe personal events in the present and near future, describe ongoing events, tell time, recognize and use numbers, and use adjectives to describe objects and others.
Produce and respond to affirmative, negative and interrogative sentences in writing using appropriate punctuation, spelling and accent marks at the elementary level.

Address others using formal and informal pronouns in the singular and plural. Recognize the variety of pronouns that exist in Spanish and the regions of the Spanish-speaking world where they are used.
Collect and provide information in real-life settings at the elementary level. Communicate preferences, likes and dislikes using spoken and written language.

Master elementary-level grammatical constructions: gender and number agreement, subject-verb agreement, and conjugation of common regular and irregular verbs in the present tense. Distinguish between present tense and past tense verbs.

Demonstrate knowledge of the variety of cultures that exist within the Spanish-speaking world. Understand the unique cultural differences among Spanish-speaking countries. Understand how language and culture reflect values, belief systems, and behavior.
